title: The Brier score
summary: How a guess becomes a score, and why 0.25 is the coin-flip line.

steps.head: Scoring a guess
steps.body: The {{brier-score|Brier score}} shows how far your number was from what happened. Lower is better.

steps.head: How it is worked out
steps.body: If the price rose, the outcome is 1. If it did not, the outcome is 0. Take your guess minus the outcome and multiply it by itself. A guess of 0.7 on a rise gives 0.3 times 0.3, which is 0.09.

steps.head: The coin-flip line
steps.body: A guess of 0.5 scores 0.25 every time, whatever happens. So 0.25 is the line to improve on.

steps.head: Being sure and wrong
steps.body: A guess of 0.9 when the price fell scores 0.81. Big, confident misses cost much more than small doubts.

steps.head: Reading your score
steps.body: A score under 0.25 over many guesses is a good sign. Over only a few guesses it may be {{luck|luck}}.
steps.more: The score screen also shows how a shuffled set of outcomes would have scored. It helps you judge luck.

questions.prompt: What is the Brier score of saying 50% every time?

options.why: Yes. 0.5 minus 1 or 0.5 minus 0 is 0.5 in size, and 0.5 times 0.5 is 0.25.
Not quite. 0.5 is the size of the gap before it is multiplied by itself.
No. A score of 0 needs a perfect guess every time.

questions.prompt: You guessed 0.9 and the price fell. About how big is the cost?

options.why: Yes. The gap is 0.9, and 0.9 times 0.9 is 0.81.
No. That is the cost of a guess of 0.7 on a rise.
No. 0.1 is the gap for a right 0.9 guess, before it is multiplied.

questions.prompt: Is a higher or a lower Brier score better?

options.why: Right. The score measures your gap from what happened, so a smaller gap is better.
No. Higher means a bigger gap from what happened.
No. The rule is the same on every day: lower is better.
